content.title: A Land Where No One Is Wronged Under Its King: The First Migration to Abyssinia
paragraphs: Chapter Sixteen
A Land Where No One Is Wronged Under Its King: The First Migration to Abyssinia

As persecution intensified in Makkah, the Muslims undertook the first migration in Islamic history: the journey to Abyssinia. It was not a journey made only by enslaved or powerless Muslims. Men and women from prominent Quraysh families also went. Some enjoyed the protection of their clans, yet Makkah had still become a place where practising their faith safely was difficult.
Hamzah and his place in the Prophet’s life

Hamzah ibn ‘Abd al-Muttalib, may Allah be pleased with him, was the Prophet’s paternal uncle and also his brother through breastfeeding. This family relationship arises when two children are breastfed by the same woman under the relevant Islamic conditions. Thuwaybah, a woman formerly enslaved by Abu Lahab and then freed, had nursed both Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, and Hamzah. Years later, when the Prophet was offered Hamzah’s daughter in marriage, he explained: “She is the daughter of my foster-brother.” — Sahih al-Bukhari 5100; Sahih Muslim 1447. Published translation excerpt: HadeethEnc, hadith 6162.

Hamzah was respected for his courage and position among Quraysh. According to the familiar Seerah account of his conversion, when he heard that Abu Jahl had insulted and harmed the Prophet ﷺ, he confronted Abu Jahl, struck him with his bow and declared that he followed Muhammad’s religion. The date of his conversion is disputed: some placed it in the second year of the mission, others closer to the sixth. Not every detail of that confrontation has an uninterrupted authentic chain. After the migration to Madinah, Hamzah would fight at Badr and be martyred at Uhud. The Prophet later accepted Islam from Wahshi, who had killed Hamzah, but asked him not to appear before him because seeing him revived his grief.

In those Makkan years, Islam had reached different Quraysh households. Its followers included vulnerable people and members of influential families alike. Yet many Muslims still could not practise their religion safely.
When Makkah became too difficult for believers

The Prophet witnessed the beatings, imprisonment, hunger and thirst inflicted on his Companions, while he himself faced abuse. His uncle Abu Talib afforded him tribal protection through relatives and a clan capable of resisting an attack. Yet Abu Talib could not protect every Muslim, and the believers possessed neither a state nor an armed force able to stop the clans from persecuting those who had embraced Islam.

According to Ibn Ishaq’s historical account, when the Prophet saw his Companions’ suffering, he advised them to seek refuge in Abyssinia, whose king allowed no one under his protection to be wronged. The account describes the country in these words: “It is moreover a land of the upright!” He advised them to remain there until Allah brought relief from their suffering. Abyssinia, a historic East African region covering areas of present-day Ethiopia and Eritrea, lay across the Red Sea. Negus, or al-Najashi, was the royal title borne by rulers of Abyssinia, not the personal name of every king. Ibn Ishaq gives this wording without a connected chain of transmitters. A related report from Umm Salamah, may Allah be pleased with her, supports the instruction to seek refuge with this just king; the migration itself is well-established history.
Why Abyssinia in particular?

Abyssinia was not the nearest possible refuge, and its ruler was then known as a Christian, not a Muslim. In the Seerah report, the decisive reason was justice: under that king, people were not wronged. Abu Talib offered his nephew protection through family ties although, according to the established hadith reports, he did not embrace Islam. The Negus had no such family relationship with the Prophet, yet justice made his country a suitable refuge. The Negus would later become Muslim, and the Prophet would perform the funeral prayer for him upon learning of his death.

The people who had not embraced Islam did not all act alike toward the new community; protection and justice mattered. Leaving still required the emigrants to part with family, homes and their own city and to cross into a country with a different language, culture and religion. For the first time, however, Muslims could establish a community beyond Makkah.
The first to leave: ‘Uthman and Ruqayyah

The first migration is commonly dated to the fifth year of the prophetic mission, although the precise dates and lists of the earliest emigrants differ across historical accounts. Among its best-known participants were ‘Uthman ibn ‘Affan and his wife Ruqayyah, the daughter of the Prophet. ‘Uthman came from Banu Umayyah, one of Quraysh’s prominent families; Ruqayyah came from the Prophet’s own household. Thus migration was neither confined to people of low social status nor a sacrifice borne by families distant from the Prophet. Other Muslims went with them, including married couples who would begin life in another land together.
Abu Hudhayfah and Sahlah: children of leading families

Abu Hudhayfah ibn ‘Utbah ibn Rabi‘ah travelled with his wife Sahlah bint Suhayl ibn ‘Amr, may Allah be pleased with them both. Abu Hudhayfah’s father, ‘Utbah, was a leading Quraysh opponent of the mission. Sahlah’s father, Suhayl ibn ‘Amr, was also a notable figure in Quraysh. Religious differences therefore divided members of the same family. In Abyssinia, Sahlah gave birth to their son Muhammad ibn Abi Hudhayfah: for some emigrants this was not a brief hiding place but a country in which their children were born.
Other emigrants in the first group

They included al-Zubayr ibn al-‘Awwam, of Banu Asad ibn ‘Abd al-‘Uzza (a branch of Quraysh to which Khadijah, may Allah be pleased with her, also belonged); Mus‘ab ibn ‘Umayr, who would later teach Islam to the people of Madinah; and ‘Abd al-Rahman ibn ‘Awf, one of the earliest believers. Abu Salamah ibn ‘Abd al-Asad went with Umm Salamah (may Allah be pleased with her), who would later become one of the Prophet’s wives, known as the Mothers of the Believers. The group also included ‘Uthman ibn Maz‘un, known for devotion and steadfastness; ‘Amir ibn Rabi‘ah and his wife Layla bint Abi Hathmah; Abu Sabrah ibn Abi Ruhm; and Suhayl ibn Bayda’.

Ibn Ishaq’s list here gives ten men and four women—Ruqayyah, Sahlah, Umm Salamah (may Allah be pleased with her) and Layla. Other source lists differ in number or membership; there is no agreement on a single list. Some Seerah accounts present ‘Uthman ibn Maz‘un as the group’s leader, but those leadership details remain historical reports of differing reliability. Crossing the sea offered believers a path other than remaining under persecution.
Why did people migrate even when not all were tortured?

Several emigrants were members of influential families. Their decision shows that migration served more than one immediate need. Some needed escape from physical abuse and imprisonment. Others needed an environment in which they could worship openly without continual social coercion. A person did not have to suffer the same physical torture as Bilal to find Makkah unliveable as a believer. At the same time, the sources do not preserve the full personal reasoning of every emigrant; the evidence does not establish one identical motive for them all. Their shared journey made communal worship possible away from Quraysh’s pressure.
The second migration: the community grows

More people followed the original party, producing a much larger migration to Abyssinia. Ibn Ishaq gives a total of eighty-three men, provided ‘Ammar ibn Yasir is counted; he himself notes uncertainty over ‘Ammar’s inclusion. Women and children were counted separately. Historical works also disagree about exact dates and how the total should be divided between the two journeys. Whatever the precise count, this was no longer a journey undertaken by a handful of people: a substantial part of the young Muslim community now lived outside Makkah, while the Prophet and others continued the mission at home.
Ja‘far and Asma’: from Abu Talib’s household to Abyssinia

Ja‘far ibn Abi Talib left with his wife Asma’ bint ‘Umays, may Allah be pleased with them both. Ja‘far was ‘Ali’s brother and the son of Abu Talib, the uncle who protected the Prophet ﷺ in Makkah. Thus even a close relative of one of the Prophet’s strongest protectors took part in the migration. Ja‘far and Asma’ joined the community in Abyssinia. Later, when Quraysh sent envoys to demand the emigrants’ return, Ja‘far would speak on their behalf before the Negus and explain Islam to him. That encounter is recounted in the chapter devoted to it.
Brothers who left the same household

Another family was that of Sa‘id ibn al-‘As, known as Abu Uhayhah, a senior Quraysh figure opposed to the mission. His son Khalid ibn Sa‘id entered Islam early, although reports differ about exactly how early. He faced his father’s opposition and migrated. His brother ‘Amr ibn Sa‘id also migrated. The Seerah records Khalid travelling with his wife, though reports differ on some details of her name, and ‘Amr leaving with his wife Fatimah bint Safwan. Khalid had children in Abyssinia, including Umm Khalid bint Khalid ibn Sa‘id, whose story would appear later. Sons of Quraysh leaders could take a different religious path from their fathers and leave Makkah because of it.

The Seerah also names ‘Abd Allah ibn Jahsh and his brother ‘Ubayd Allah ibn Jahsh among families allied with Banu Umayyah through a pact of mutual protection rather than necessarily through descent. ‘Ubayd Allah emigrated with Umm Habibah bint Abi Sufyan (may Allah be pleased with her). Many kinship groups and alliances therefore converged in Abyssinia; it was not the refuge of just one tribe.
Seven brothers whose names are little known today

The biographical collections, which record people’s lineages and notable events in their lives, also preserve accounts of seven sons of al-Harith ibn Qays, named among the early Muslims and emigrants, although some identifications and details differ by source. Abu Qays ibn al-Harith migrated in the second group, later participated at Uhud and was martyred at al-Yamamah. His brother ‘Abd Allah ibn al-Harith migrated too; he was known for poetry and was likewise martyred at al-Yamamah. Al-Sa’ib ibn al-Harith emigrated; some accounts place his injury at al-Ta’if and his death at the battle of Fihl, a place in present-day Jordan where the battle occurred during the early conquests. Al-Hajjaj ibn al-Harith migrated and was later martyred at al-Yarmuk according to Ibn Sa‘d; other reports place his martyrdom at Ajnadayn. Sources differ over the fifth brother’s name: Tamim or Bishr ibn al-Harith; few other details survive. Sa‘id ibn al-Harith migrated and was martyred at al-Yarmuk. Ma‘bad ibn al-Harith, called Ma‘mar in another report, is also named, although less is preserved about his life.

These are more than names in an old register. Each person left Makkah when the Muslim community was small, and each subsequently followed a different path. Some lived through events of the Prophet’s lifetime, some survived into the later conquests, and some were martyred at al-Yamamah, al-Yarmuk or elsewhere. Biographical sources disagree on certain details, which remain uncertain.
A community that remained abroad for years

The immediate purpose of the migration was safety and the ability to practise Islam. Yet some Muslims remained in Abyssinia for many years. While some returned earlier, Ja‘far and a group with him only reached the Prophet in the seventh year after the migration to Madinah, around the opening of Khaybar. Why did they not all return as soon as the Prophet migrated to Madinah—or after the victory at Badr? The sources establish that some stayed abroad, but do not give an explicit individual reason for every emigrant.

One possible interpretation is that maintaining a Muslim group in a safe country offered an additional refuge while the community in Arabia remained exposed. The sources do not establish this as a policy of the Prophet or the emigrants. Danger persisted after Badr, including the battles of Uhud and al-Ahzab. Ja‘far’s return occurred at a very different stage of Muslim history from the first departure out of Makkah.
Allah’s earth is vast

The Qur’an says: «O My believing slaves, My earth is spacious, so worship Me alone.» (29:56). Worship need not be tied to one homeland when a believer is unable to practise the faith there and is able to move.

The Qur’an says: «Those who migrated for the sake of Allah after being oppressed, We will surely give them good in this world. But the reward of the Hereafter is greater, if only they knew,» (16:41). Allah promises a place where the emigrants can settle. In meaning, the verse promises a good abode to those who emigrated for Allah after suffering wrong, while their reward in the next life is greater. Al-Tabari reports Qatadah’s explanation connecting the verse to Muslims oppressed in Makkah, some of whom left for Abyssinia before Madinah became another place of migration. This is an interpretive report, not an authentic prophetic hadith identifying the verse’s revelation with one named emigrant.

The Qur’an says: «Whoever emigrates for the sake of Allah will find on earth many places of refuge and abundant provision. Whoever leaves his home emigrating for the cause of Allah and His Messenger, then death overtakes him, his reward has already been secured with Allah. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.» (4:100). The places of refuge are places where emigrants can escape their oppressors and find room to live. The verse promises that whoever migrates in Allah’s cause will find refuge and abundance; if death overtakes that person after leaving home for Allah and His Messenger, the reward remains with Allah. Some reports connect it to emigrants to Abyssinia, but the surah is Madinan and Ibn Kathir discusses these attributions. The verse has a general meaning; its revelation concerning a particular emigrant to Abyssinia is not established.
A Muslim community in a new land

The migrants came from different families and social circumstances: ‘Uthman and Ruqayyah; Abu Hudhayfah and Sahlah; Abu Salamah and Umm Salamah (may Allah be pleased with her); al-Zubayr, Mus‘ab and ‘Abd al-Rahman; ‘Uthman ibn Maz‘un; ‘Amir and Layla; and many others. They were followed by Ja‘far and Asma’, members of great Quraysh households, and lesser-known early believers. Emigration reduced one form of persecution but demanded separation from home, relatives and the Prophet, and life in an unfamiliar country.

The Prophet continued preaching in Makkah while a group of Companions lived under a ruler reputed to be just. Quraysh, however, did not simply abandon those who had escaped its authority. It would try to reach them abroad and demand their return. At that moment Ja‘far ibn Abi Talib would have an important encounter with the Negus—an encounter recounted in the chapter devoted to it.
Principal sources for this chapter

• Ibn Ishaq’s Seerah, as transmitted by Ibn Hisham. The quoted description of Abyssinia follows Osman Nûri Topbaş, The Prophet Muhammad Mustafa the Elect, translated by Süleyman Derin and Erdinç Atasever (Erkam Publications, 2022), p. 216; the rest of the advice is narrated indirectly. For the distinction between Ibn Ishaq’s wording without a connected chain and Umm Salamah’s related report: al-Albani, al-Silsilah al-Sahihah 3190, 7:577–578, citing al-Bayhaqi, al-Sunan al-Kubra 9:9 and Dala’il al-Nubuwwah 2:301. The emigrants’ stay in Abyssinia is also attested in Sahih al-Bukhari 4230.

• Hamzah’s breastfeeding relationship: Sahih al-Bukhari 5100 and Sahih Muslim 1447. For the differing dates of his conversion and his participation at Badr and martyrdom at Uhud: Ibn ‘Abd al-Barr, al-Isti‘ab, Hamzah’s biography, entry 541, 1/369–375. For Wahshi’s account: Sahih al-Bukhari 4072; Ibn al-Mulaqqin’s al-Tawdih, 21/181, explains the aversion to seeing the person who killed a loved one.

• The migrations, participant names and counts: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham and Ibn Kathir’s al-Bidayah wa’l-Nihayah; the names and numbers of the earliest group vary between sources. See Ibn Hisham, 1/322–324, for the first group and the families of Ja‘far, Khalid, ‘Amr and the Ibn Jahsh brothers; 1/330 gives eighty-three men while noting uncertainty over ‘Ammar’s inclusion. Ibn Kathir, al-Bidayah wa’l-Nihayah, 4/165–169, attributes the fifth-year dating to al-Waqidi and discusses differing lists and sequences of departure. The date given here is drawn from these historical reports.

• Details of the sons of al-Harith ibn Qays: Ibn Sa‘d, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra, al-Khanji edition, 4/181–183, entries 428–434; entry 434 records the Ma‘bad/Ma‘mar variant. For al-Sa’ib at al-Ta’if and Fihl: Ibn ‘Abd al-Barr, al-Isti‘ab, entry 885. For the Yarmuk/Ajnadayn alternatives concerning al-Hajjaj: Ibn ‘Asakir, Tarikh Dimashq, 12/93–96, entry 1205.

• Qur’anic passages: al-‘Ankabut 29:56; al-Nahl 16:41 with Qatadah’s view in al-Tabari; al-Nisa’ 4:100 and Ibn Kathir’s discussion of some proposed occasions of revelation. The three Quran quotations follow the Rowwad Translation Center edition published by QuranEnc (29:56; 16:41; 4:100).

A Muslim community in a new land

The migrants came from different families and social circumstances: ‘Uthman and Ruqayyah; Abu Hudhayfah and Sahlah; Abu Salamah and Umm Salamah (may Allah be pleased with her); al-Zubayr, Mus‘ab and ‘Abd al-Rahman; ‘Uthman ibn Maz‘un; ‘Amir and Layla; and many others. They were followed by Ja‘far and Asma’, members of great Quraysh households, and lesser-known early believers. Emigration reduced one form of persecution but demanded separation from home, relatives and the Prophet, and life in an unfamiliar country.

The Prophet continued preaching in Makkah while a group of Companions lived under a ruler reputed to be just. Quraysh, however, did not simply abandon those who had escaped its authority. It would try to reach them abroad and demand their return. At that moment Ja‘far ibn Abi Talib would have an important encounter with the Negus—an encounter recounted in the chapter devoted to it.
Principal sources for this chapter

• Ibn Ishaq’s Seerah, as transmitted by Ibn Hisham. The quoted description of Abyssinia follows Osman Nûri Topbaş, The Prophet Muhammad Mustafa the Elect, translated by Süleyman Derin and Erdinç Atasever (Erkam Publications, 2022), p. 216; the rest of the advice is narrated indirectly. For the distinction between Ibn Ishaq’s wording without a connected chain and Umm Salamah’s related report: al-Albani, al-Silsilah al-Sahihah 3190, 7:577–578, citing al-Bayhaqi, al-Sunan al-Kubra 9:9 and Dala’il al-Nubuwwah 2:301. The emigrants’ stay in Abyssinia is also attested in Sahih al-Bukhari 4230.

• Hamzah’s breastfeeding relationship: Sahih al-Bukhari 5100 and Sahih Muslim 1447. For the differing dates of his conversion and his participation at Badr and martyrdom at Uhud: Ibn ‘Abd al-Barr, al-Isti‘ab, Hamzah’s biography, entry 541, 1/369–375. For Wahshi’s account: Sahih al-Bukhari 4072; Ibn al-Mulaqqin’s al-Tawdih, 21/181, explains the aversion to seeing the person who killed a loved one.

• The migrations, participant names and counts: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham and Ibn Kathir’s al-Bidayah wa’l-Nihayah; the names and numbers of the earliest group vary between sources. See Ibn Hisham, 1/322–324, for the first group and the families of Ja‘far, Khalid, ‘Amr and the Ibn Jahsh brothers; 1/330 gives eighty-three men while noting uncertainty over ‘Ammar’s inclusion. Ibn Kathir, al-Bidayah wa’l-Nihayah, 4/165–169, attributes the fifth-year dating to al-Waqidi and discusses differing lists and sequences of departure. The date given here is drawn from these historical reports.

• Details of the sons of al-Harith ibn Qays: Ibn Sa‘d, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra, al-Khanji edition, 4/181–183, entries 428–434; entry 434 records the Ma‘bad/Ma‘mar variant. For al-Sa’ib at al-Ta’if and Fihl: Ibn ‘Abd al-Barr, al-Isti‘ab, entry 885. For the Yarmuk/Ajnadayn alternatives concerning al-Hajjaj: Ibn ‘Asakir, Tarikh Dimashq, 12/93–96, entry 1205.

• Qur’anic passages: al-‘Ankabut 29:56; al-Nahl 16:41 with Qatadah’s view in al-Tabari; al-Nisa’ 4:100 and Ibn Kathir’s discussion of some proposed occasions of revelation. The three Quran quotations follow the Rowwad Translation Center edition published by QuranEnc (29:56; 16:41; 4:100).
